title: No. 26 — The Idea of Restraining the Legislative Authority in Regard to the Common Defense Considered. (Hamilton)
paragraphs: It could hardly be expected that, in a popular revolution, men's minds would stop at that happy mean which marks the beneficial boundary between POWER and PRIVILEGE and combines the energy of government with the security of private rights. A failure on this delicate and important point is the great source of the problems we now experience. If we are not careful to avoid repeating the error in our future attempts to correct and improve our system, we may travel from one fantastic project to another and try change after change, yet never be likely to make any material change for the better.

The idea of restraining the legislative authority in the means of providing for the national defense is one of those refinements that owe their origin to a zeal for liberty more ardent than enlightened. We have seen, however, that it has not so far been widely accepted. Even in this country, where it first appeared, Pennsylvania and North Carolina are the only two States that have favored it to any degree, and all the others have refused to give it the least support. They wisely judged that confidence must be placed somewhere, that the necessity of doing so is implied in the very act of delegating power, and that it is better to risk an abuse of that confidence than to hamper the government and endanger the public safety by unwise restrictions on the legislative authority. In this respect the opponents of the proposed Constitution fight against the general decision of America. Instead of being taught by experience to correct any extremes we may have run into before, they seem ready to lead us into others still more dangerous and more extravagant. As if the tone of government had been found too high or too rigid, the doctrines they teach are calculated to lower or relax it by expedients that, on other occasions, have been condemned or avoided. It may be affirmed, without any charge of invective, that if the principles they teach on various points were to prevail so far as to become the popular creed, they would utterly unfit the people of this country for any kind of government whatever. But a danger of this kind is not to be feared. The citizens of America have too much discernment to be argued into anarchy. And I am much mistaken if experience has not produced a deep and solemn conviction in the public mind that greater energy of government is essential to the welfare and prosperity of the community.

It may not be amiss here to remark briefly on the origin and progress of the idea that aims at excluding military establishments in time of peace. In speculative minds it may arise from contemplating the nature and tendency of such institutions, reinforced by events in other ages and countries. But as a national feeling, it must be traced to the habits of thinking we inherit from the nation from which the inhabitants of these States have in general descended.

In England, for a long time after the Norman Conquest, the authority of the monarch was almost unlimited. Inroads were gradually made on the prerogative in favor of liberty, first by the barons and afterward by the people, until the greater part of its most formidable claims died out. But it was not until the revolution of 1688, which raised the Prince of Orange to the throne of Great Britain, that English liberty completely triumphed. As an incident of the undefined power of making war, which was an acknowledged prerogative of the crown, Charles II had, on his own authority, kept a body of 5,000 regular troops on foot in time of peace. James II increased this number to 30,000, who were paid out of his civil list. At the revolution, to abolish the exercise of so dangerous an authority, an article was included in the Bill of Rights then drawn up, that "the raising or keeping a standing army within the kingdom in time of peace, UNLESS WITH THE CONSENT OF PARLIAMENT, was against law."

In that kingdom, when the pulse of liberty was at its highest pitch, no security against the danger of standing armies was thought necessary beyond a prohibition on raising or keeping them up by the mere authority of the chief executive. The patriots who brought about that memorable revolution were too temperate and too well informed to think of any restraint on the legislative discretion. They knew that a certain number of troops for guards and garrisons was indispensable; that no precise limits could be set to national emergencies; that a power equal to every possible contingency must exist somewhere in the government; and that, when they referred the exercise of that power to the judgment of the legislature, they had reached the furthest point of precaution that was consistent with the safety of the community.

It is remarkable that even in the two States that seem to have contemplated a ban on military establishments in time of peace, the wording used is cautionary rather than prohibitory. It is not said that standing armies SHALL NOT BE kept up, but that they OUGHT NOT to be kept up in time of peace. This ambiguity of wording appears to have resulted from a conflict between jealousy and conviction: between the desire to exclude such establishments at all events and the belief that an absolute exclusion would be unwise and unsafe.

Can it be doubted that such a provision, whenever the state of public affairs was understood to require a departure from it, would be interpreted by the legislature as a mere admonition and made to yield to the necessities, or supposed necessities, of the State? Let the fact already mentioned about Pennsylvania decide. What, then, it may be asked, is the use of such a provision, if it ceases to operate the moment there is an inclination to disregard it?

Let us examine whether there is any comparison, in effectiveness, between the provision I have mentioned and the one in the new Constitution that limits appropriations of money for military purposes to a period of two years. The former, by aiming at too much, is bound to accomplish nothing. The latter steers clear of an imprudent extreme and is perfectly compatible with proper provision for the nation's emergencies, so it will have a beneficial and powerful effect.

By this provision the legislature of the United States will be OBLIGED, at least once in every two years, to deliberate on whether it is proper to keep a military force on foot, to come to a new resolution on the point, and to declare its view of the matter by a formal vote in the face of its constituents. It will not be AT LIBERTY to give the executive department permanent funds for the support of an army, even if it were incautious enough to be willing to place so improper a confidence in it. Since the spirit of party, in different degrees, must be expected to infect all political bodies, there will no doubt be persons in the national legislature ready enough to challenge the measures and accuse the intentions of the majority. The provision for supporting a military force will always be a favorable subject for declamation. Every time the question comes up, the opposition party will rouse the public's attention and draw it to the subject. If the majority should really be disposed to exceed the proper limits, the community will be warned of the danger and will have an opportunity to take measures to guard against it. Apart from parties in the national legislature itself, every time the period of discussion arrives, the State legislatures will have their attention awake to the conduct of the national rulers. They will always be not only vigilant but suspicious and jealous guardians of the citizens' rights against encroachments from the federal government, and if anything improper appears they will be ready enough to sound the alarm to the people, and to be not only the VOICE but, if necessary, the ARM of their discontent.

Schemes to overthrow the liberties of a great community REQUIRE TIME to mature for execution. An army large enough to menace those liberties seriously could be formed only by gradual additions. That would suppose not merely a temporary combination between the legislature and the executive but a continued conspiracy over a period of time. Is it probable that such a combination would exist at all? Is it probable that it would be persisted in and passed along through all the successive changes in a representative body that elections every two years would naturally produce in both houses? Is it to be presumed that every man, the instant he took his seat in the national Senate or House of Representatives, would begin as a traitor to his constituents and to his country? Can it be supposed that there would not be found one man discerning enough to detect so atrocious a conspiracy, or bold or honest enough to inform his constituents of their danger? If such presumptions can fairly be made, there ought at once to be an end of all delegated authority. The people should resolve to take back all the powers they have so far parted with, and to divide themselves into as many States as there are counties, so that they may manage their own concerns in person.

Even if such suppositions could reasonably be made, it would still be impracticable to conceal the design for any length of time. The very act of enlarging the army to so great an extent in time of profound peace would announce it. What plausible reason could be given, in a country so situated, for such vast additions to the military force? It is impossible that the people could be deceived for long, and the destruction of the project and of its projectors would quickly follow the discovery.

It has been said that the provision limiting appropriations for the support of an army to a period of two years would be useless. The argument is that the Executive, once in possession of a force large enough to awe the people into submission, would find in that very force resources enough to do without supplies from acts of the legislature. But the question comes up again: on what pretense could he be put in possession of a force of that size in time of peace? If we suppose it to have been created because of some domestic insurrection or foreign war, then the case falls outside the principles of the objection, which is aimed at the power of keeping up troops in time of peace. Few people will be so visionary as to contend seriously that military forces ought not to be raised to put down a rebellion or resist an invasion. And if the defense of the community in such circumstances should make it necessary to have an army so numerous as to put its liberty at risk, this is one of those calamities for which there is neither prevention nor cure. It cannot be provided against by any possible form of government. It might even result from a simple league, offensive and defensive, if the confederates or allies were ever required to form an army for common defense.

But it is an evil far less likely to befall us in a united state than in a disunited one. Indeed, it may safely be asserted that it is an evil altogether unlikely to befall us in the latter situation. It is not easy to imagine that dangers so formidable could assail the whole Union as to require a force large enough to put our liberties in the least jeopardy, especially if we take into account the aid to be had from the militia, which ought always to be counted on as a valuable and powerful auxiliary. But in a state of disunion, as has been fully shown elsewhere, the opposite supposition would become not only probable but almost unavoidable.
